body: The earliest known drawing made by humans is generative. Ochre cross-hatching found at Blombos Cave in South Africa is the earliest known drawing yet found anywhere. “They qualify as generative because the placement of individual marks has not been decided by the artisan, but dictated by a manually executed symmetry‐based algorithm,” according to Philip Galanter.

Casey Reas has spoken of how logical, systems thinking is “really essential for this medium.” What the Blombos cave art and many other similar, prehistoric tiling patterns reveal is the ancient, innate and unmistakably human origins of systems thinking in art.

Blombos Cave’s symmetry-based tiling system may not universally be considered autonomous and thus generative. As I argue, the critical question to ask is: “Does the artist relinquish control to an external system at some point?” While a simple tiling system is deployed here, more complex versions will appear later in our story with Islamic tile art.

cite.label: Paul, Christiane. A Companion to Digital Art, 159. John Wiley & Sons Inc, 2019.

body: Oldest known evidence of basket weaving dates back to c. 24,000 BCE. Impressions of weaving on fired clay found in Moravia, Central Europe, predating settled life. Some studies suggest the practice could be much older and origins of the practice are unclear. This algorithmic process is widely considered a generative practice, for example, by Nettrice Gaskins. This ancient practice continues to inspire artists to this day.

img.cap: A coiled reed basket from New Kingdom Egypt — a contextual image of the coiling technique, not the Upper Palaeolithic evidence itself.
img.credit: Basket, Egypt, ca. 1550–1300 BCE, coiled basketry. The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York, Rogers Fund, 1925 (Open Access / CC0).

body: The first author known by name was a woman: Enheduanna (fl. ca. 2300 BCE), daughter of Akkadian king Sargon and high priestess at the temple of the moon god in Ur, southern Mesopotamia. Her collection of Temple Hymns bears an inscription that translates, roughly, to: “The compiler of this tablet is Enheduanna. That which I’ve created has never existed before.” -Sasha Stiles

Babylonians are first to understand applied geometry, using triangles to parcel farmland and track celestial bodies. The Greeks would build upon these concepts with roots in logic and eventually Euclid’s Elements.

First written between 1,000 to 750 BCE, I Ching, also known as the Book of Changes, is an ancient Chinese divination text. Some interpret the complex text to have introduced the binary system, based on its two symbols, the broken (yin) and solid (yang) lines, representing darkness and light respectively. This Western interpretation of the I Ching as binary may not be consistent with the document’s original meaning yet has impacted mathematics, philosophy and—thousands of years later—modern technology. In that sense, the I Ching was later read as an early form of binary.

The formative figure and avid reader of Chinese texts, Gottfried Leibniz, who is also discussed later in this chapter, would go on to document the binary system in his 1703 paper, “Explanation of Binary Arithmetic.” In the paper, through his perhaps flawed interpretation of the I Ching, Leibniz draws comparisons between his binary system and the Fuxi hexagram arrangement Bouvet sent him, citing it several times and employing its identifiable hexagrams.

According to Dr. Andreas Schöter, I Ching’s system of symbols can be interpreted as binary representation. Schöter argues that the versatile system has inspired both historical and contemporary computational thinkers. Additionally, several prominent generative artists have been inspired by the I Ching throughout the previous decades, including John Cage, Manfred Mohr and Marius Watz.

For millennia, reaching back to at least 4200 BCE, Andean textiles have woven together stories of identity and ancestral beliefs. Predating written languages, textiles served as the predominant medium for conveying images and concepts, often including striking geometric patterns. These intricate cloth creations continue to hold profound significance to the Andean worldview to this day.

img.cap: An embroidered Paracas border fragment from the south coast of Peru, its repeating figural and geometric bands worked in camelid hair on cotton.
img.credit: Border Fragment, Paracas, 450–175 BCE. The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York, Bequest of Arthur M. Bullowa, 1993 (Open Access / CC0).

body: Scholars and travelers flock to Delphi, the most important shrine in Ancient Greece, to ask questions about the future and await, in exchange for gold and gifts, enigmatic replies from the Pythia, priestess of Apollo. The deep-rooted impulse toward oracular dialogue, the intellectual exercise of deciphering the Pythia’s statements, and the cultural significance of such prophetic divinations lays a foundation for contemporary search engines and predictive text engines that tap into our collective consciousness, offering sometimes puzzling, sometimes profound answers. -Sasha Stiles

Pythagoras credited with popularizing geometrical patterns, “the main feature of 1960s computer art. Computer artworks were frequently based on the golden section, Fibonacci numbers, and many other emblematic Pythagorean premises,” according to Grant Taylor.

cite.label: Taylor, Grant D. When the Machine Made Art: The Troubled History of Computer Art, 76. New York: Bloomsbury Academic, 2014.

body: Considered one of the most influential and long-used textbooks of all time, Elements remains a key work in geometry’s logical development. Euclid’s ancient Greek text consists of thirteen books that demonstrate how to make logical proofs to ascertain certainty and investigate the unknown. The books also include some of the earliest known algorithms. The concepts Elements introduced would be critical in the development of algorithms by Islamic mathematicians and throughout the European Middle Ages. The text would again prove vital in early modern science, influencing Copernicus, Kepler and Galileo among countless others. Its legacy throughout the millennia is unquestioned. Like the seminal advancements in binary systems from I Ching, Elements played a critical role in moving the field of logic forward. Binary systems and logic would prove foundational to modern attempts to design computing machines, including by Gottfried Leibniz later in this chapter.

Library of Alexandria is established around the mission of “holding in one place all of the knowledge ever accumulated by man,” the world’s “memory bank”; the Ptolemic dynasty grows the library by decreeing that any book brought into the city be immediately copied by scribes, and taking measures to preclude rivals from collecting books. -Sasha Stiles

Hero of Alexandria, Greek mathematician and engineer, created a number of automata, including the aeolipile, a steam turbine, a fountain, a wind-powered organ and a puppet theater. Some of the earliest known mechanical devices, Hero’s automata demonstrated advanced knowledge of physics and engineering, paving the way for future developments in automation and robotics.

Islamic geometric patterns, emerged in the 8th century during the Islamic Golden Age, influenced by Greek, Roman and Sasanian Persian mathematics and ornament. An example of a generative process predating the computer, Islamic artists used these complex geometric shapes to create intricate, symmetrical designs that were used to decorate buildings, manuscripts, textiles, and other objects.

The Persian Al-Khwārizmī's Concerning the Hindu Art of Reckoning introduced zero, the decimal system and Hindu numerals to the Islamic and European world from India. Preserved only in its Latin translation, the text was likely based on Arabic translations of the Indian mathematician Brahmagupta’s work. Al-Khwārizmī’s name, Algoritmi in Latin, later led to the term “algorithm" when the text reached European readers through twelfth-century Latin translations.
It was also during this time of the Abbasid Caliphate, considered a “golden age,” that Islamic tiling and other abstract geometric forms flourished.

body: Ramón Llull’s logic machine was a device used to generate new knowledge by mechanically combining concepts and ideas. It anticipated the concept of computation, inspiring later philosophers and scientists to explore the potential of machines for generating new knowledge. The logic machine also had practical applications in fields such as language translation and cryptography. This device was highlighted in Cybernetic Serendipity as an important development in the history of the digital computer.

Englishman Richard of Wallingford designs the St Albans astronomical clock, an early clockwork machine. An example of a generative process predating the computer, the art of creating clockwork figures became more refined during the Renaissance period, from the 15th to the 17th century, when some of the most complex and intricate automata were created.

Johannes Gutenberg begins developing the mechanised moveable type printing press that would kick off Europe’s Printing Revolution, capable of producing up to 3600 pages per day and significantly reducing the cost of publishing and distributing literature. This innovation would lead to the era of mass communication, enabling information and ideas to circulate widely and transcend the elite’s monopoly on literacy. -Sasha Stiles
Luca Pacioli’s book, illustrated by Leonardo, helped popularize the principles of mathematical proportion and beauty, known as the Golden Ratio, in art and architecture.

Packed with meaning and symbols, Melencolia I features a depiction of Dürer’s solid (the eight-faced stone to the left) whose points form the Dürer graph. The solid is a geometric shape discovered by Dürer and used in his art. It was instrumental to the development of perspective and proportion in art history as well as these mathematical concepts in geometry. In the top right we see the “magic square” where the numbers in each row, column, diagonal and quadrant all add up to 34.

This work was highly influential to Vera Molnár. She developed systematic variations on the “magic square” from this piece. Molnár first encountered Dürer at the age of 14 or 15 and would say this about her experience to Hans Ulrich Obrist: “That was something very important to happen upon Dürer’s magic square in Melancholia. I was very young and was looking for a foundation, something that I could hold onto in making non-figurative painting." Here, Molnár reveals how Melencolia led her to abandon figurative work for good.
Continuing, Molnár explains how her experience with Dürer led her to focus on the abstract, beginning a life-long love affair with the square:

“I was looking for a rule, something hidden, a secret, and felt that I’d found it in the magic squares system.... The magic square was like that. I liked Dürer’s work very much. As I was courageous, hard-working and methodical, I said to myself that I would try with other magic squares.”

Centuries before the Turing test, we have the Descartes test. In René Descartes' Discourse on the Method published originally in 1637, as the preface to three essays; an English translation followed in 1649.

In its fifth part he imagines machines built to look and move like humans and gives two tests that would still expose them, saying: "For we may easily conceive a machine to be so constructed that it emits vocables, and even that it emits some correspondent to the action upon it of external objects which cause a change in its organs; for example, if touched in a particular place it may demand what we wish to say to it; if in another it may cry out that it is hurt, and such like; but not that it should arrange them variously so as appositely to reply to what is said in its presence, as men of the lowest grade of intellect can do."

So Descartes had two tests. The first is language. Such a machine might respond in human-like ways but Descartes was skeptical that such a machine could ever arrange their responses generally. The second is versatility across all of life's tasks. Natural language processing and conversational programs dating back to Joseph Weizenbaum’s ELIZA and including today’s LLMs still answer to Descartes bar: replying sensibly to whatever is said.

body: It was the first mechanical calculator made in quantity, performing addition and subtraction with an automatic carry between digits. Using a series of gears and wheels, the calculator revolutionized mathematics and engineering, paving the way for further development of machines that could perform more complex calculations. Pascal’s calculator was mentioned in the catalog of Cybernetic Serendipity as an important moment in the history of cybernetics.

Leibniz’s Dissertatio de arte combinatoria (“On the Combinatorial Art” 1666) was one of several cornerstone papers he would write throughout his life on concepts such as symbols, binary systems and formal logic. His voluminous writing and tinkering with machines would prove hugely influential to the development of computing.

“On the Combinatorial Art” expanded his habilitation thesis at Leipzig. In it, he proposed a system of using symbols and rules to combine ideas and discover new knowledge. His system for arranging and manipulating concepts to find answers sounds remarkably similar to what we call algorithms.

In addition to this seminal text, Leibniz decades later published the paper, “Explanation of Binary Arithmetic," in which he is credited for inventing the binary system. Leibniz also made important contributions to the field of formal logic before inventing several mechanical computational devices. His ability to synthesize knowledge throughout the ages to contribute to modern computing make him a singular figure in our story.

Also known as the “stepped reckoner,” this was an early mechanical calculator, demonstrated in wooden model form to the Royal Society in 1673, designed to perform all four arithmetic operations. It was an important advancement in the field of computation, paving the way for further developments in the design and construction of calculating machines, including the development of digital computers.
In John Peter’s book Artificial Versifying, the English mathematician describes a simple procedure that could be used to make generative poetry in Latin.

Meant as fun for children, the procedure involved selecting letters in a way to produce grammatically and metrically correct poems without any prior knowledge of the language. This system stands as one of the earliest examples of generativity used in a creative endeavor. John Clark would go on to build the Eureka machine between 1832 and 1845, based on Peter’s Artificial Versifying.

img.cap: John Peter, the six versifying tables from Artificial Versifying, first edition, London: John Sims, 1677.
img.credit: John Peter / John Sims, 1677. Reproduction: Kaeden Berg, Henry Koelling and James Ryan, “English Versification for the Billion,” ELO 2021, figure 2, via ELMCIP. Original scan photographer not identified. Image source.
img.alt: Six numbered grids of Latin letters and dark stopping cells used to generate hexameter verse.
creator: John Peter

body: In Gulliver’s Travels, “the Engine” is a device that shuffles words into new combinations, essentially serving as a prototype for a mechanical text generator. “The Engine” is one of the earliest references to a device resembling the modern computer.

Benjamin Motte published the book in London in1726. The Engine appears in Part III, at the Academy of Lagado, where pupils turn iron handles to rearrange wooden blocks bearing words, so that “the most ignorant person” might write books. Sound Familiar?

Known as Musikalisches Würfelspiel (“musical dice game”), this method first published by Johann Philipp Kirnberger was a monumental event in the history of art and chance. The game was a musical composition technique in which pre-composed measures were selected by rolls of dice. Serving as one of the earliest examples of aleatoric (chance) music, it stands as one of the earliest examples generally of art generated randomly by chance. Many subsequent, famous composers would experiment with musikalisches würfelspiel, including C.P.E. Bach and, by attribution, Mozart, who is still the most known practitioner. Musikalisches würfelspiel also begin the tradition of generative music developing prior to graphics, which continued into the twentieth century with Max Mathews at Bell Labs developing MUSIC I nearly a decade before computer graphics were exhibited as art.

img.credit: Johann Philipp Kirnberger / George Ludewig Winter. Bavarian State Library copy, reproduced via Wikimedia Commons; scan photographer unidentified. Image source.

body: Thomas Bayes developed this statistical framework, published posthumously by Richard Price, allowing for the quantification of uncertainty and the updating of probabilities based on new evidence. It has wide applications in fields such as artificial intelligence and data science. It contributed to the development of machine and deep learning when in 1964 Ray Solomonoff combined Bayesian probability-based reasoning and theoretical computer science to make predictions based on the past. Solomonoff and Andrej Kolmogorov would go on to expand upon information theory—discussed more in chapters 3 and 4—to develop Occam’s razor, a key concept to neural networks.
We've been trying to make human-like machines for centuries.

In 1783 Karl Gottlieb von Windisch published letters describing exactly such a thing: a chess-playing automaton built by his friend Wolfgang von Kempelen for the Habsburg court in the decade prior. The machine, a life-size figure in Turkish dress seated at a cabinet, beat many challengers across Europe. Windisch's book, issued in German and French immediately and in English the next year as Inanimate Reason, praised it without claiming to know how it worked: “'Tis a deception! granted; but such an one as does honor to human nature.”
The deception was apparently a strong human player hidden inside, which Edgar Allan Poe argued in his 1836 essay “Maelzel's Chess-Player.”

img.cap: A copperplate engraving of Kempelen's chess-playing automaton, the Turk, seated at its cabinet.
img.credit: Engraving of Wolfgang von Kempelen's chess player from Karl Gottlieb von Windisch, Briefe über den Schachspieler des Hrn. von Kempelen (1783). Wikimedia Commons.

body: The Jacquard loom used punch cards to control the weaving of patterns in fabric. It introduced the notion of a program stored outside the machine on punch cards, which would later result in generative weaving and modern computing. Charles Babbage would go on to utilize Jacquard’s method of punch card programming as one of computing’s earliest pioneers. “Computers did not pave the way for generative art; generative art helped to pave the way for computers,” according to Phil Galanter. Punch card programming would continue developing for the next century and a half before culminating in the use of mainframe computers and early languages such as FORTRAN. Additionally, textile design has continued to influence both fine art as well as generative art to this day. Examples include the Bauhaus weaving workshop’s Anni Albers and Gunta Stölzl, the quilters of Gees Bend, Anna Lucia, Travess and Andreas Rau.

cite.label: Paul, Christiane. A Companion to Digital Art, 151. John Wiley & Sons Inc, 2019.

body: As mechanization rose throughout the globe in the nineteen century, much like AI is today, we faced similar fears of humanity's power to construct its own intelligent beings. Thankfully, in the twenty-first century, that fear has entirely disappeared. Oh. Isaac Asimov would go on to name the fear the novel dramatizes the “Frankenstein complex.”

We know about the fears of people two hundred years ago through their art and culture like, Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus which was published anonymously in London in three volumes on January 1, 1818. Mary Wollstonecraft Shelley had begun it in the summer of 1816 near Geneva, when Lord Byron proposed that each member of his party, including Mary and her husband Percy Bysshe Shelley, write a ghost story.

The story itself if well known. Scientist, Victor Frankenstein, assembles a living being and ultimately their relationship sours. The "monster" learns language by listening in secret and turns on its maker.
Many further such stories have been told, including films like The Terminator and the Matrix. But humanity's ability to create its own destruction has been persistent fear in our psyche.

body: ‍Photography’s impact on modern art is well established but its impact on digital and computer art more specifically is less examined yet central to this story. According to Herbert W. Franke, "The most significant stage on the path to the mechanization of the fine arts has been photography.” Further, art critic Frank Popper includes photography as the first of seven influences on the development of digital art. Digital generative artists such as Casey Reas, Margot Lovejoy and Terry Gips have all stressed the importance of photography to the development of computer art as well.

Nicéphore Niépce produced the earliest photograph made in a camera obscura that survives today, using a pewter plate coated with bitumen. This breakthrough served as the basis for the continuation of developments in photography to this day. The invention of photography stands as a paradigm shift in art history. The camera’s ability to capture representations of the visible world would lead to painters losing interest in strict realism and spur the gradual abstraction of modern art. Photography, in addition to becoming its own art form, would also lead to cinema and video art, as art expanded from a handmade practice to include capture practices.

cite.label: Franke, Herbert W. Computer Graphics, Computer Art, 93. Berlin: Springer, 1985.

body: Foundational to the development of cybernetics, this unrealized mechanical computer aimed to use punch cards, inspired by the Jacquard Loom, to perform calculations.
One of the earliest designs for a programmable computer, it also had a significant impact on the development of modern computers and programming languages.
In her 1843 notes on Babbage's Analytical Engine, Lovelace wrote that the machine could originate nothing and only do what it was ordered to do. Turing answers the objections by name in 1950.
This prescient observation hints at the different paths computation would take from hard-programmed rules to learning models.
People: Ada Lovelace.

img.cap: A watercolor portrait of Ada Lovelace by Alfred Edward Chalon, about 1840.
img.credit: Alfred Edward Chalon, Ada King, Countess of Lovelace, c. 1840, watercolor. Science Museum Group, London, via Wikimedia Commons.

body: Computer programming is born, as Ada Lovelace’s 1843 notes on Charles Babbage’s Analytical Engine set out a program for computing Bernoulli numbers, making her the first published computer programmer. Her work demonstrated the potential for computers to perform complex tasks, foreshadowing the development of modern programming languages. She even envisioned the computer’s ability to create programmed art. Inspired by the notion of combining science and art, Lovelace recognized the computer’s ability to extend beyond calculating numbers. She understood its potential to create complex images and music by translating basic rules into symbolic logic, carrying on the traditions of Euclid, Al-Khwārizmī and Leibniz. Lovelace foresaw a future where computers could be programmed to create beautiful and imaginative works of art, envisioning a creative partnership between humans and machines. This concept anticipated the field of computer-generated art by over a century. Her prescient ideas have inspired generations of computer programmers and artists. Lovelace would inspire future women pioneers in the field of programming such as Grace Hopper who introduced the use of natural language in programming in the 1950s.
The "notes" accompany Lovelace's 1843 English translation of Luigi Federico Menabrea's French memoir on the Engine. However, the notes actually run about three times as long as the memoir.

The Harmonograph, commonly agreed to be invented by Hugh Blackburn, is a mechanical apparatus that creates geometric drawings, typically Lissajous-type figures, through the use of pendulums. It stands as an early example of an autonomous system/machine that generates artistic forms, and as a precursor to later generative art and computer graphics.

img.credit: Wikipedia. 2023. "Harmonograph." Wikimedia Foundation. Last modified February 2, 2023. en.wikipedia.org.

body: John Clark’s Latin verse generating machine, Eureka, was a full mechanized version of John Peter’s book, Artificial Versifying, from 1677 and earlier in this Timeline.

The machine generated Latin hexameter verse and stands as a precursor to the typewriter and other early mechanical devices. The inventor John Clark spent thirteen years building Eureka, from 1832 to 1845, which resembles a bookcase. This early automatic machine combined science, mechanization, computation, randomness and art in a way that is recognizable to contemporary digital generative art.
The device stands as another example of the roots of generative poetry often stretching back further than generative graphics.

cite.label: Sharples, Mike. "John Clark's Latin Verse Machine: 19th Century Computational Creativity." IEEE Annals of the History of Computing 45, no. 1 (2023): 31-42.
